item.title: llama.cpp and AMD Launch Benchmark Dashboard for Local AI Inference
item.description:
llama.cpp and AMD Launch Benchmark Dashboard for Local AI Inference

The llama.cpp project and AMD have released a new benchmark dashboard for measuring local inference performance on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Available on Hugging Face, the dashboard enables developers to track prompt processing and text generation performance across different llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations.

📊 Overview

The dashboard is designed to make performance comparisons straightforward for AMD developers. Users can select specific hardware, models, and llama.cpp builds to compare quantizations and follow performance changes over time.

Key features include:

  • Tracking PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens)
  • Build history tab to monitor performance across all recorded builds
  • Context scaling tab to observe how token-generation throughput changes as context grows
  • Access to underlying benchmark results through public workflows

⚙️ Key Details

| Component | Description | |—|—| |————| | Hardware Options | Radeon 8060S (gfx1151), Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201) | | Test Metrics | PP512 and TG128, both starting at context depth zero | | Benchmark Frequency | Weekly public workflows | | Model Set | Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models | | GGUF Formats | Q4_K_M, Q8_0, BF16, F16 |

The benchmark workflows run with Flash Attention enabled and disabled, using 10 repetitions per configuration. Performance is measured as mean throughput (avg_ts) for both PP512 and TG128 tests.

🚀 Availability

The dashboard is hosted on Hugging Face and reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket. Users can click the data source link beside each chart title to access the underlying JSONL files for specific build, hardware, and model combinations.

Standard results follow the path format ///.jsonl, while workload sweeps use -tg.jsonl filenames.

💡 Why It Matters

This tool provides transparent, accessible performance data for local AI inference on AMD hardware, helping developers optimize their deployments and understand the impact of different quantization strategies and hardware configurations.

#llama.cpp #AMD #benchmarking #local-inference

Source: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

item.title: Simple Python bindings for llama.cpp released
item.description:
Simple Python bindings for llama.cpp released

Simple Python bindings for the llama.cpp library are now available, providing low-level access to the C API via ctypes and a high-level Python API for text completion.

🧩 How it works

The package allows developers to integrate llama.cpp into Python environments with several key interfaces:

  • Low-level access: Direct access to the C API through a ctypes interface.
  • High-level API: A Python API designed for text completion.
  • OpenAI-like API: Compatibility with standard OpenAI-style interfaces.
  • Framework Support: Includes compatibility with LangChain and LlamaIndex.
  • Web Server: Features an OpenAI compatible web server.

⚙️ Key details

The server component supports a range of additional capabilities, including:

  • Function Calling support
  • Vision API support for multimodal models
  • Configuration and multi-model support
  • Local Copilot replacement for code completion

Installation requires Python 3.8+ and a C compiler. The build process compiles llama.cpp from source and installs it alongside the Python package. Hardware acceleration backends are supported via specific environment variables:

  • OpenBLAS: Set GGML_BLAS and GGML_BLAS_VENDOR.
  • CUDA: Set GGML_CUDA=on. Supported CUDA versions include 11.8, 12.1, 12.2, 12.3, 12.4, 12.5, 13.0, or 13.2. GPU compute capability requirements vary by version: 6.0–8.9 for CUDA 11.8, 6.0+ for CUDA 12, and 7.5+ for CUDA 13. Pre-built wheels for CUDA support Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12.
  • Metal (MPS): Set GGML_METAL=on. Requires macOS 11.0 or later.

All llama.cpp cmake build options can be configured via the CMAKE_ARGS environment variable or the --config-settings / -C CLI flag during installation.

🚀 Availability

Documentation is available at https://llama-cpp-python.readthedocs.io/en/latest. Installation is supported on Linux (gcc or clang), Windows (Visual Studio or MinGW), and MacOS (Xcode).

#llama.cpp #Python #Llama #LocalLLM #CTypes

Source: abetlen/llama-cpp-python

item.title: ROS 2 Packages Integrate llama.cpp for LLM and VLM Support
item.description:
ROS 2 Packages Integrate llama.cpp for LLM and VLM Support

A new set of ROS 2 packages has been released to integrate the llama.cpp library into ROS 2 environments. This repository allows developers to incorporate llama.cpp’s optimization capabilities into ROS 2 projects to run various machine learning models.

🧩 How it works

The llama_ros packages enable the execution of GGUF-based models within a ROS 2 framework. The supported model types include:

  • Large Language Models (LLMs)
  • Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
  • Audio-language models
  • Embedding models
  • Reranking models

⚙️ Key details

Beyond basic model execution, the packages provide specific interfaces and features derived from llama.cpp:

  • An OpenAI-compatible chat completions interface that supports tool calling, reasoning, and streaming.
  • Speculative decoding.
  • Support for decision models, including OpenJEV, Lev, Kev, Nimble, Laya, and Clef.
  • Grammar-based generation (GBNF).
  • Real-time modification of LoRAs.

#ROS2 #llama.cpp #LLM #ROS #GenerativeAI

Source: mgonzs13/llama_ros

item.title: llama.cpp v1.0.0 supports LLM inference across hardware
item.description:
llama.cpp v1.0.0 supports LLM inference across hardware

llama.cpp is a C/C++ project for LLM and MLLM inference, with v1.0.0 listed. Its stated goal is to enable inference with minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of hardware, locally and in the cloud.

🔍 Overview

The project is built on the ggml library. It lists Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF among its model references, as well as text-to-speech (TTS) models and GBNF grammars.

⚙️ Usage

After installation, the provided command to run Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF is:

1

llama cli -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF

The project also provides a command to launch an OpenAI-compatible API server:

1

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF

The listed interfaces include the llama-server REST API and the lib llama API.

🚀 Availability

Installation options listed for llama.cpp include:

  • Visit https://llama.app and follow the instructions.
  • Run with Docker, using the Docker documentation.
  • Download pre-built binaries from the releases page.
  • Build from source by cloning the repository and following the build guide.

The project lists Docker, Winget, Nightly, Server, Release, and an MIT license.

🤝 Contributing

Contributors can open PRs. Collaborators are invited based on contributions, and maintainers can push to branches in the llama.cpp repo and merge PRs into the master branch. The project points contributors to CONTRIBUTING.md for more information.

#llama.cpp #LLMInference #C++ #GGUF

Source: ggml-org/llama.cpp

item.title: Hugging Face Releases llama.cpp v1.0.0 and ggml v1.0.0 Libraries
item.description:
Hugging Face Releases llama.cpp v1.0.0 and ggml v1.0.0 Libraries

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face has released v1.0.0 of both the llama.cpp and ggml libraries, marking a significant milestone 3.5 years after the project’s inception.

🔍 Overview

With growing adoption and many downstream applications depending on the project, version 1.0.0 establishes a flexible and stable API standard. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml, alongside all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning, will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps.

⚙️ Released Libraries

Library Function
llama.cpp v1.0.0 LLM inference in C/C++
ggml v1.0.0 Tensor library for machine learning

🧩 How it works

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across hardware ranging from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers.

  • Inference Accessibility: Uses quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation to deliver accessible AI inference across the software stack.
  • Dynamic Backends: ggml implements dedicated backends that can be compiled as dynamic libraries and optionally loaded at runtime to run on virtually any hardware.
  • Hardware Collaborations: Features hardware support and self-hosted runners from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM, and Intel.
  • Model Compatibility: Supports continuous integration for all model architectures, currently covering over 150 architecture variants alongside mainstream speculative decoding methods.

🛠️ Infrastructure and Quality

  • Development priorities include maintaining a high-quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture, and understanding implementation details.
  • CI infrastructure uses Hugging Face technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs to scale capacity and guarantee correctness for changes landing on master branches.
  • The team continues to thoughtfully integrate LLMs into its own development cycle.

🚀 Availability

  • Llama desktop applications are available for MacOS and Windows, shipped by the llama.cpp team and Hugging Face.
  • The team plans to expand software distribution methods to reach more developers and end-users.

#llamacpp #ggml #HuggingFace #OpenSourceAI #MachineLearning

Source: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

item.title: Serving llama.cpp Decision Models on SageMaker with Text and Structured Paths
item.description:
Serving llama.cpp Decision Models on SageMaker with Text and Structured Paths

Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure.

🔍 Overview

  • Two deployment paths are available from the same packaged model (Figure 1).
  • Text‑generation path uses the AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI‑compatible chat completions API.
  • Structured‑decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options.

🧩 How it Works

Standard text‑generation path

  1. Package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon S3.
  2. Reference the published AWS DLC image for llama.cpp directly.
  3. At container start, the DLC scans /opt/ml/model for the first .gguf file.
  4. The container maps POST /invocations to llama‑server at /v1/chat/completions.
  5. SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables are passed as arguments to llama.cpp.

Structured‑decision path (SemIf)

  1. Use AWS CodeBuild to build a child image that keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries.
  2. Replace the default entry point with a SageMaker‑compatible SemIf adapter.
  3. Store the child image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).
  4. The adapter reads the final‑position logits and state that the llama‑server API does not expose, and returns a decision schema with option_ids, probabilities, option_logits, plus prompt, timing, and model metadata.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema.
  • Generated text is found in choices[0].message.content of the response.
  • SemIf uses a constrained decision schema (no chat messages) and returns:
    • option_ids
    • probabilities
    • raw option_logits
    • prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata.
  • Stable option IDs let applications apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing free‑form text.
  • SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application‑defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations mentioned are Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model, Kev, and Strands Decider 2B.

🚀 When to Use Which Path

  • Standard text‑generation – Use when you need OpenAI‑compatible chat completions via InvokeEndpoint.
  • Structured‑decision (SemIf) – Build a child image only when you need direct access to logits or state, such as:
    • Routing a case to a specific queue
    • Extracting a single value from a known set
    • Assigning incident priority
    • Checking a policy outcome
    • Selecting an agent action
  • Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model and validate probabilities before treating them as operational confidence.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The managed SageMaker AI path removes the need to run custom inference servers for quantized llama.cpp models.
  • By swapping in a SemIf adapter, the same model can serve both free‑form text and structured decision outputs, reducing model duplication.
  • Applications gain deterministic, audit‑ready probabilities while still leveraging a single underlying LLM.

#SageMaker #llama.cpp #SemIf #AIInference #DecisionModels

Source: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: llama.cpp v0.4.0 Released with 18 Backends and 1-Bit Quantization
item.description:
llama.cpp v0.4.0 Released with 18 Backends and 1-Bit Quantization

The llama.cpp project, a pure C/C++ LLM inference engine, has released stable version v0.4.0 on 2026-09-04, alongside a rapid cadence of 12 nightly builds in approximately 27.5 hours. The release extends the engine’s reach with 18 backend directories and introduces experimental 1-bit quantization, furthering its goal of “minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of hardware.”

🔍 Overview

llama.cpp is an inference engine built on the ggml library. Its README states the goal up front: LLM (and VLM) inference “with minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of hardware.” The latest stable release, v0.4.0 on 2026-09-04, is the only numbered release among the last 100; everything else is b108xx nightly builds pouring out with merges. Public since 2023-03-10, the cadence has held for over three years.

🧩 How it works

The engine uses a modular backend system. The ggml/src/ directory holds 18 matching backend directories. A registry in ggml/src/ scans, loads libraries, and picks the highest-scoring backend — each backend advertises its own capability in the same header, and the dispatcher trusts only that number.

For models larger than total VRAM, the README describes a hybrid mode: part runs on GPU, the rest falls back to CPU.

⚙️ Key details

Quantization support

The README lists the range — 1.5-bit, 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, 5-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit integer quantization “for faster inference and reduced memory use.” Most striking is IQ1_S/IQ1_M — super-block 1-bit quantization: each weight keeps roughly one bit of information, and the model still generates tokens.

The enum in ggml.h spans 1-bit (IQ1_S/M), 4-bit (Q4_K, MXFP4) to 8-bit (Q8_0) — 56 type definitions in one header.

All compression kernels live in ggml-quants.c — 5,667 lines of C.

Supported backends

The “Supported backends” table in the README lists 17 backends — from CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, and HIP to Hexagon for Snapdragon, WebGPU for browsers, and even IBM zDNN.

Model format

The models doc says it plainly: “requires the model to be stored in the GGUF file format” — other formats must be converted with the Python scripts shipped in the repo. The key-value structure is so lean the API is declared in just 211 lines of gguf.h — a spec you can read in one sitting.

Contribution policy

The repo governs AI contributions with a “100% responsible for every line” policy and ships its own contribution-guidance skill in-tree. The first principle: “AI-generated code is allowed. What is not allowed is submitting code you do not understand.” Contributors own 100% of every line, whoever typed it — because every merged line is maintained indefinitely by a small maintainer team across a vast platform-backend matrix.

Measurement tools

Alongside sit the measurement tools: tools/quantize to compress, tools/imatrix to measure an importance matrix before compressing, tools/perplexity and tools/llama-bench to verify quality after — compress, then measure; never compress and trust.

🚀 Availability

Stable release v0.4.0 on 2026-09-04, yet 12 nightly b108xx builds landed in ~27 hours (per GitHub API on 2026-09-08). The repo’s pushed_at falls in the same window — 11:36:37 UTC on 2026-09-08.

💡 Why it matters

llama.cpp aims for performance across a “wide range of hardware” — x86, Apple Silicon, down to phone NPUs. With 18 backends and quantization as low as 1-bit, it enables running LLMs on devices that lack dedicated GPUs, while the hybrid GPU/CPU mode handles models larger than total VRAM. Inference configs for local LLMs are provided, including ready-to-run settings for Ollama Modelfile, vLLM command, and llama.cpp itself.

#llama.cpp #localAI #quantization #opensource #AIinference

Source: llama.cpp: efficient LLM inference from CPU to the edge — wakii Source: Ollama, vLLM and llama.cpp configs for local LLMs · Contexte Tech

item.title: Transformers Now Supports llama.cpp GGUF Quantizations for Local Inference
item.description:
Transformers Now Supports llama.cpp GGUF Quantizations for Local Inference

The Transformers library now allows users to run llama.cpp GGUF quantizations using from_pretrained, enabling AI model generation directly on a user’s own machine.

🔍 Overview

GGUF is a widely used format for local inference developed by the llama.cpp team. It packages model weights and metadata—including tokenizer information and optional chat templates—into a single file. This format supports various quantization levels, allowing users to reduce the memory footprint by trading off some precision.

🧩 How it works

To achieve performance close to llama.cpp, Transformers reuses its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library and reduces overhead in generate.

  • Loading: Users pass the Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.
  • Execution: On Apple Silicon, when weights stay packed on Metal, Transformers automatically loads compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn for attention implementation.
  • Fallbacks: If the compatible kernel cannot be fetched, the system falls back to “sdpa” (which can also be forced by passing attn_implementation="sdpa"). Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader dequantizes the model, which uses more memory.

⚙️ Key details

Initial focus is on local inference for Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture. Users can select different quantization variants based on their available memory:

Quantization Variant Description
Q4_K_M Mixes tensor precisions; uses mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.
Q5_K_M Recommended for users with more memory available.
Q6_K Recommended for users with more memory available.

🚀 Availability

Ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints are available on the Hub from several providers:

  • ggml-org
  • Unsloth
  • LM Studio Community
  • bartowski

💡 Why it matters

Running AI models locally has been made practical through llama.cpp and projects like MLX. The llama.cpp inference engine already powers tools such as Ollama, Jan, and LM Studio. Integrating this into Transformers makes it easier to run these models locally while allowing the same endpoint to be used by other clients that support the API.

#Transformers #llama.cpp #GGUF #LocalAI #AppleSilicon

Source: Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants
